transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-10-12
Time: 15:00 UTC / 08:00 PT
Duration: ~41 minutes
Attendees: Lena Ortiz (Redwood AE), Marcus Reed (Redwood SE), Aisha Khan (CTO - Silver Sparrow), Tom Li (Platform Eng)

Auto Summary: quick notes auto-generated - Silver Sparrow evaluating Redwood for public API that needs 99th percentile latency < 350ms for 256 token responses, cost sensitivity for high qps, needs SOC2 and KMS integration, interested in pilot credits.

[00:00:00] Lena (Redwood AE): Hi everyone, thanks for taking the time, this is Lena on the account side, with Marcus our SE. Could we do quick intros?
[00:00:10] Aisha (Silver Sparrow): Hey Lena, hi Marcus. I'm Aisha, CTO, Tom is our platform lead, we're trying to figure out how quickly we can get from prototype to live.
[00:00:18] Tom (Silver Sparrow): Morning. We have an internal API gateway and run services on GCP, primarily.
[00:00:25] Marcus (Redwood SE): Great. Quick agenda—understand your traffic profile, latency targets, security needs, and then we can map hosted vs dedicated vs private. If there's time we'll talk quickstart credits and ttft, time-to-first-token.
[00:00:36] Aisha: Sounds good. Our main requirement is customer-facing NLU for product search and small completions. We need p95 < 200ms ideally, p99 under 350. We're at about 250 RPS during peaks and want to plan for 1k RPS in six months.
[00:00:50] Tom: We do about 30–40% of requests that are >= 512 tokens; average is ~270 tokens. We're also sensitive to cost, we run tight unit economics.
[00:01:06] Lena: That's helpful. Quick question on data residency or compliance—do you need a VPC/private install, or is hosted okay behind contractual controls?
[00:01:14] Aisha: For initial pilot, hosted is fine if you provide SOC2 and contractual assurances. For enterprise rollout we may need VPC/private or dedicated with customer-managed KMS. Also need audit logs and SAML SSO for admin.
[00:01:27] Marcus: We support Hosted API with SOC2 and encrypted rest, Dedicated pools with reserved capacity and dedicated GPUs, and Private (VPC or on-prem) which supports customer KMS/HSM and private control plane. For latency—small answer: hosted often fastest to TTFT because no infra setup; dedicated gives predictable throughput and lower jitter. Private gives full isolation but longer onboarding.
[00:01:48] Tom: Can you quantify expected latency differences? If we move from hosted to dedicated what delta are we seeing?
[00:01:55] Marcus: It depends on model and sequence length. For a 256-token completion on a medium-size quantized model, hosted p99 might be ~250–400ms depending on region and load. Dedicated with pinned capacity will reduce jitter and often shave 20–40% off p99 latency under steady-state. But if you need single-digit tens of ms at tail we'd usually recommend smaller context models or model distillation. There's also batching/caching—prefix/KV cache helps reduce per-token work for chat-like flows.
[00:02:20] Aisha: We do have a lot of repeated prefixes for search re-rank flows, so prefix caching would help. Do you do automatic KV cahce? (sic)
[00:02:28] Marcus: Yes, we have automatic prefix and KV cache which can be configured per-route to keep hot keys in memory and reduce token compute. There was a small typo in our docs that said KV cache — sometimes transcribed as KV cahce, sorry.
[00:02:36] Lena: On cost—we usually show unit economics: tokens plus the model type, plus any dedicated infra premiums. For pilots we can provide credits; for example we often offer $3k–$10k quickstart credits depending on scope.
[00:02:47] Tom: What's the typical flow for getting to first token? Our engineers are stretched, want to know how much effort on our side.
[00:02:55] Marcus: For hosted quickstart with our SDK it's typically under 2 hours to a hello-world integration and under a day to baseline end-to-end with auth and tracing. We can provision API keys and a test project; we also provide sample workload harnesses to run latency tests.
[00:03:07] Aisha: Great. Do you have an SDK for Go? Our service is in Go and Kotlin.
[00:03:12] Lena: We have official SDKs for Node and Python; Go and Java are community SDKs but we have maintained examples and a short Go snippet we can share. Marcus: I can drop a Go example repo link in the follow-up.
[00:03:24] Tom: How does rate limiting and quotas work? We need per-customer throttling.
[00:03:29] Marcus: Per-route quotas, API keys tied to projects, and token-level cost breakdown in the console. For Dedicated you can configure per-tenant throughput mapping.
[00:03:38] Aisha: Security—SOC2 is required, and we need to encrypt data at rest with our KMS for Private. Also need to know retention windows for training-data opt-out.
[00:03:47] Lena: We have SOC2 type II; we'll send the cert and security pack. For Private deployments we can integrate with your KMS/HSM; hosted has customer-controlled workspace-level deletions and retention policies. Training-data opt-out is configurable and we can provide audit logs.
[00:03:58] Tom: Any special networking? We run GCP and would prefer a VPC peering or private link.
[00:04:03] Marcus: For Dedicated and Private we support VPC peering and private endpoints. Hosted can be used over standard TLS endpoints; for strict egress controls Private is the path.
[00:04:12] Aisha: Ok let's talk scale—if we hit 1k RPS with burstier traffic, what's recommended?
[00:04:18] Marcus: For high sustained RPS, reserved Dedicated pools are best—you get predictable concurrency, autoscaling rules, and burst buffers. You can also route low-latency critical traffic to a smaller low-quant model and bulk workloads to larger cheaper models. There are also routing policies to fallback to cheaper siblings when capacity constrained.
[00:04:34] Tom: Any mention of quantization? We're open to int8 if performance is there.
[00:04:38] Marcus: We recommend quantization for cost; our runtime supports quantized paths and we've got kernel selection tuned per hardware. For many workloads int8 or int4 can cut cost 2–3x with acceptable quality drop; we can recommend model variants after seeing your evals.
[00:04:52] Aisha: How would we validate quality delta? We have a set of prompts and human evals.
[00:04:57] Marcus: That's perfect—send us representative prompts and we'll run a comparison matrix with baseline model, quantized variants, and compute-latency tradeoffs. That will also be the basis of the benchmark.
[00:05:07] Lena: For commercial terms—pilot credits, then monthly usage billing for hosted; for Dedicated we do a reserved capacity contract with monthly invoice and SLAs. Private usually has a platform fee plus support tiers. I'll share standard templates.
[00:05:19] Tom: Any common objections you see? Customers worry about vendor lock-in.
[00:05:23] Marcus: We hear that; our approach is to provide model versioning, exportable model artifacts (where applicable for Private), and standard HTTP APIs so you can migrate. We also support canary rollouts and A/B to limit blast radius.
[00:05:34] Aisha: Okay practical next steps?
[00:05:37] Lena: We propose: 1) We send the security pack & SOC2 2) Provision $5k quickstart credits 3) Marcus runs the 2K-token latency benchmark against your sample traces and returns numbers 4) Follow-up technical check on Oct 19. Does that work?
[00:05:53] Tom: Yes. For the benchmark, we'll add a dataset of 200 representative calls and expected throughput profile, and we'll capture traces via our gateway.
[00:06:02] Marcus: Perfect, please send them to me via the secure upload link, we'll load into our harness.
[00:06:10] Aisha: One more question—what about SSO for admin console? We use SAML 2.0 and SCIM for provisioning.
[00:06:16] Lena: We support SAML SSO and SCIM provisioning for user sync in the console; for Dedicated/Private we also have RBAC and optional audit retention windows.
[00:06:24] Tom: Any docs on pricing vs batch size and latency?
[00:06:28] Marcus: Yes, we have a pricing doc that maps token cost per model and examples for batching strategies—larger batches improve throughput but increase tail latency for single requests; we'll send a short spreadsheet with simulated unit economics.
[00:06:42] Aisha: That would help decision makers.
[00:06:45] Lena: I'll include the pricing sheet and a quick runbook for ttft—how to get the first token in under a day, plus sample curl and Go snippets.
[00:06:53] Tom: Anything else on the support side? SLA?
[00:06:56] Lena: Dedicated customers get SLA-backed uptime and latency targets in the contract; hosted customers have standard availability terms and we offer premium SLAs as an add-on. Support tiers can be added for on-call coverage.
[00:07:07] Marcus: Quick note—for realistic latencies you should test from your infra region to our region endpoints; cross-region adds 50–80ms sometimes. We'll note that in the benchmark.
[00:07:18] Aisha: Makes sense. One small nit—our finance team will want to understand commitment sizes; what's the minimum Dedicated commit?
[00:07:24] Lena: Typical minimum is a monthly reserved capacity commitment, often starting at a few thousand dollars per month depending on GPU mix; I'll include ballpark numbers in the pricing sheet. If you want we can model an ingress scenario for 6 months to show break-even.
[00:07:38] Tom: Okay, that helps.
[00:07:40] Lena: Any final questions?
[00:07:43] Aisha: Not right now. We'll get the sample traces to Marcus and expect the credit provisioning.
[00:07:49] Marcus: Great, I'll follow up with a benchmark plan and a short checklist for the traces.
[00:07:54] Lena: Thanks all, recap: security pack + SOC2, $5k credits, Marcus to run benchmarks, follow up 2026-10-19. We'll put items into the CRM.
[00:08:03] Tom: Thanks, bye.
[00:08:05] Aisha: Bye.
